concept: Cash and carry basis trade returns and risks
summary: Source-anchored research for Cash and carry basis trade returns and risks. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Glassnode data, relayed by TFTC and Cryptonomist on 3 August 2026, says the 3-month annualized BTC futures basis had paid less than the 2-year US Treasury since February 2026, and that only one other stretch on record ran this long (August 2022 to January 2023). Cryptonomist adds about 3% against about 3.8% and 157 consecutive days; TFTC gives no figures. Both articles rest on one Glassnode source (the Week 30 2026 'Paid to Wait' report and a Telegram post) that was not retrieved directly, and the comparison pairs a 3-month basis with a 2-year yield. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-03)

BIS states cash-and-carry is risky because margins spike and positions can be liquidated during drawdowns. This is a limit to arbitrage and lets high carry persist. Practitioner explainers describe the same 'right but early' failure: the basis can widen before it converges, and a margin call can force an exit at a loss even though the trade would have paid at expiry. (medium confidence)

Kaiko/Amberdata name four main risks of the crypto carry trade: exchange counterparty risk (funds sit on exchange), execution slippage at scale, funding-rate variability on perpetuals, and basis volatility. Practitioner guides add that unified (cross-asset) margin can tie the whole account to its weakest position under stress. (medium confidence)

The trade's economic viability is judged against the risk-free rate plus capital and counterparty costs, not against zero. The Block frames the trade as unattractive once basis yield falls below the risk-free rate plus those costs. Kaiko/Amberdata likewise proposes staying in T-bills when its carry score is low. Gross basis alone overstates net return. (medium confidence)

Unified (cross-asset) margin and venue-local price oracles add stress risk to a hedged book. FTI says unified margin ties portfolios to their weakest assets. It also says USDe traded in the mid-$0.60s on Binance on 10 October 2025 while staying near $1 elsewhere, so margin engines that used Binance's own price marked collateral down and liquidated accounts that would have stayed solvent under cross-venue pricing. Single source. (low confidence)

Cash-and-carry means long spot (or a spot ETF) plus short a dated future. If the future trades above spot, the premium is the locked-in profit, and it converges to zero at expiry. CME bitcoin futures are cash-settled against a reference rate, so the spot leg is never delivered. Position P&L equals the premium captured minus any widening of the basis before expiry (P&L = minus the change in futures-minus-spot), so basis compression helps the holder and basis widening hurts. The P&L identity is a derivation consistent with BIS's description of the risk. (high confidence)

The trade is risk-free only at convergence. While it is open the basis can widen, for example when trend followers add long futures, so the short leg shows mark-to-market losses, draws margin calls and can be liquidated before maturity even though the trade would have paid at expiry. Practitioner sources describe the same 'right but early' problem and add exchange counterparty risk, perpetual funding swings and slippage at scale. CryptoSlate says calling the trade 'riskless' overstates it. (high confidence)

Practitioners judge the trade against the risk-free rate plus costs, not against zero. The Block says the trade is dead when basis yield drops below the risk-free rate plus capital costs, and saw 'essentially zero incentive' at about 5% against about 4.5%. Kaiko/Amberdata calls more than 10% excess over T-bills attractive and less than 3% not worth it, and advises staying in T-bills when its carry score is low. CryptoSlate lists funding, margin, fees, execution, spot financing and balance-sheet costs as what erases the gross spread. These thresholds are vendor heuristics, not tested rules. (medium confidence)

Hedge funds cut ETF positions as carry fell in late 2025. CF Benchmarks reports that the top hedge-fund holders of IBIT cut holdings from about 114 million shares in Q3 2025 to 82 million in Q4 2025 (-28%), including Brevan Howard from 37.5 million to 5.5 million shares. It attributes the cuts to the October 2025 blow-off top and the basis compression that followed. Kaiko/Amberdata and Spark likewise attribute part of the Q4 2025 ETF outflows to basis-trade unwinds rather than directional selling, but none of the three sources measures that share. (medium confidence)

BIS attributes the size and variation of crypto carry mainly to a volatile convenience yield, driven by trend-chasing small investors who want leveraged upside and by a shortage of arbitrage capital willing to run cash-and-carry. Interest rate differentials explain very little of the variation. (high confidence)
